one_liner: Asynchronous C++17 logger whose LOG_INFO call site costs single-digit nanoseconds, about 45x below async spdlog at p50.
what_it_does: Quill is an asynchronous logging (and metrics) library: the calling thread binary-serializes the log arguments into a per-thread queue and a single backend worker thread formats them with a bundled {fmt} and writes them to sinks (console, rotating files, JSON, Android, custom). The API is macro-based (LOG_INFO(logger, "fmt {}", x), LOGV_* for named variables, rate-limited LOG_*_LIMIT) with an optional slower macro-free function API; it is not a drop-in for spdlog, though the {fmt} format strings carry over. Loggers and sinks are created through quill::Frontend and the worker is started with quill::Backend::start().
how_it_is_fast: Each producer thread owns a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue, so there is no shared state or contention between logging threads. The call site stores only a timestamp (rdtsc by default), a pointer to static constexpr metadata (format string, source location), a logger pointer, a pointer to a templated decode function and a raw binary copy of the arguments; all {fmt} formatting, pattern formatting and I/O is deferred to the backend thread, which merges the per-thread queues in timestamp order. spdlog's async logger, by contrast, formats the message on the caller before queueing it.
when_to_use: Latency-critical hot paths (trading, real-time control, game servers) where the caller thread must spend under ~20 ns per log call with ints, doubles and short strings.
Multi-threaded producers: per-thread SPSC queues keep p99.9 at 17-18 ns with 4 threads in the author's harness, where async spdlog reaches 1106 ns.
Logging STL containers and large strings on the hot path: vector<string> of 16 strings costs 53 ns p50 versus 6906 ns for spdlog and about 750 ns for fmtlog/XTR.
Projects that want human-readable text logs plus a broad feature set (rotation, JSON, backtrace ring buffer, MDC, filters, Prometheus metrics) rather than a binary log format.
Linux, macOS, Windows, BSD or Android targets with a C++17 compiler and packaging through vcpkg, Conan, Homebrew, Meson, Bazel or Conda.
when_not_to_use: Raw text throughput is the goal: in the same harness XTR writes 7.73M msg/s versus Quill's 6.44M, and MS BinLog (61.79M) and BqLog (12.86M) binary modes are far ahead if you accept offline decoding.

Memory-constrained processes with many logging threads: every thread gets its own queue (131,072 bytes default, growing in unbounded mode), and a third-party BqLog benchmark reported multi-GB peak use at 10 threads.

You need every message delivered under overload without blocking: the bounded dropping queue (used for the headline numbers) discards messages when full, and the unbounded queue trades that for memory growth.
Programs that log from static/global destructors or fork() after starting the backend: the README documents both as unsafe.
Synchronous logging where the message must be on disk before the call returns; Quill is built around a background worker and an explicit flush_log().

integration.dependencies: none external (bundles {fmt} as the fmtquill namespace; links Threads; stdc++fs on GCC < 9)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.12+ (experimental C++20 named module optional)
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD/BSD, Android; rdtsc clock on x86 with chrono/system clock alternatives
integration.thread_safety: Logging from any thread is safe; each thread gets its own SPSC queue and one backend thread consumes them all.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same {fmt} format-string syntax as spdlog, but a different setup API (Frontend/Backend, sinks) and LOG_* macros taking a logger pointer; user-defined types need codecs or the quill/std/*.h headers for STL types.

gotchas: Arguments are copied at the call site and formatted later on the backend thread, so user-defined types need a codec (or must be formatted to a string first) and STL types need their quill/std/*.h include.

Queue type and capacity are compile-time FrontendOptions; the README benchmark ran the bounded dropping queue at 262,144 bytes, twice the default, and benchmark builds use the macro API, which is faster than the function API (11 versus 6 ns p50).
Quill's own singletons are function-local statics: logging from destructors of static objects can touch destroyed state, and calling Backend::start() before fork() breaks the child.
Messages from different threads are reordered by timestamp on the backend with a configurable grace window, so late producers can appear out of strict order unless that window is tuned.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Quill over fmtlog or XTR when you log containers or long strings (53 ns vs about 750 ns for vector<string>) or want rotation, JSON, MDC and metrics in one maintained package; pick MS BinLog or BqLog binary mode instead for maximum throughput if offline decoding is acceptable, and PlatformLab NanoLog only if you can live with its binary log and preprocessor.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's public logger_benchmarks harness (GCC 14.2, Release, -march=x86-64-v3, Intel Core i5-12600 on a tuned RHEL 9.4 with isolcpus and mitigations=off), a LOG_INFO with two ints and a double costs 6/9 ns (p50/p99.9) on one thread with Quill's bounded dropping queue versus 271/360 ns for spdlog's async_logger (8M-slot thread pool, block overflow policy, basic_file_sink_st), and 8/18 versus 557/1106 ns with 4 threads; each observation averages 20 back-to-back calls timed with serialized rdtsc. Backend throughput writing 4M messages to a file was 6.44M msg/s versus spdlog's 2.57M.
status_note: Actively maintained (v13 line, 3.0k stars, last commit 2026-10-04, CI on Linux/macOS/Windows/BSD with sanitizers and fuzzing), MIT-licensed and header-only, so it is easy to adopt through any major package manager.
